hook.line: Two friends both say *if I have time*. One will probably show up and the other won't, and the verb after *si* is how you tell which is which.
hook.es: Si tengo tiempo, voy a Taganga.
hook.en: If I have time, I'll go to Taganga.

examples.en: If I have time, I'll go.
If I had time, I'd go.
If I arrive early, I'll help you. (to a friend)
If I arrived early, I'd help you. (to a friend)

examples.es: Si hace sol, vamos a la playa.
examples.en: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach.

examples.es: Si hiciera sol, iríamos a la playa.
examples.en: If it were sunny, we'd go to the beach.

rule:
Ask yourself one question: *could this really happen?*

Yes, it is a real possibility: *si* + the ordinary present, and the result in the present too.
*Si hace sol, vamos a la playa.* (It might well be sunny.)

No, it is imaginary, or very unlikely: *si* + the *ra* form, and the *would* form for the result.
*Si hiciera sol, iríamos a la playa.* (It isn't sunny, or you doubt it will be.)

Same words, same sentence; only the verbs change, and with them how likely you think it is. English does this with *is* versus *were*, but often blurs it. Spanish makes you choose every time.

Never mix the sets: a real *if* gets a real result, an imaginary *if* gets an imaginary one.
smallPrint: Teachers call the first kind a real or open condition and the second an unreal condition (*condicional real* and *irreal*).

options: If I have time, I'll go to the beach.
If I had time, I'd go to the beach.
I had time and went to the beach.
If I arrived early, I'd help you.
If I arrive early, I'll help you.
I arrived early and helped you.

If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *tengo* or *tuviera* and type the whole sentence. Real possibility: *Si ___ tiempo, voy.* (If I have time, I'll go.)
yourTurn.why: It might really happen, so the ordinary present.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *voy* or *iría* and type the whole sentence. Imaginary: *Si tuviera tiempo, ___.* (If I had time, I'd go.)
yourTurn.why: An imaginary *if* needs the *would* form in the result.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: If it's sunny, we'll go to the beach.
yourTurn.answer: Si hace sol, vamos a la playa.
accept: Si hace sol, iremos a la playa.
yourTurn.why: Sunny is a real possibility, so *si* + *hace*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: If it were sunny, we'd go to the beach.
yourTurn.answer: Si hiciera sol, iríamos a la playa.
accept: Iríamos a la playa si hiciera sol.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it imaginary: *Si llego temprano, te ayudo.* (If I arrived early, I'd help you. To a friend.)
yourTurn.why: Both verbs move to the imaginary set: *llegara* and *ayudaría*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it real: *Si supiera la respuesta, te la diría.* (If I know the answer, I'll tell you. To a friend.)
yourTurn.answer: Si sé la respuesta, te la digo.
yourTurn.why: A real possibility takes the ordinary present in both halves.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: If I had time, I'd help you. (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: I don't have time, so it is imaginary: *tuviera* and *ayudaría*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. An imaginary *if* needs an imaginary result, so *iría*.
A real *if* gets a real result: don't switch to the *would* form halfway.
Never put the *would* form after *si*; use the *ra* form.

personal: Say one real plan and one daydream about the same thing: *Si tengo tiempo, …* and *Si tuviera tiempo, …*. Something true about you.
